newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African bank secrecy laws need reviewing - Manuel.
newsitem.headline: S.African bank secrecy laws need reviewing - Manuel.

text.p: Bank secrecy laws needed to be re-examined to prevent money laundering without endangering client-bank confidentiality, South African Finance Minister Trevor Manuel said on Tuesday.

Speaking during the second reading debate on the South African Reserve Bank Amendment Bill which allows for greater disclosure by the central bank on rescue operations, Manuel said that bank secrecy laws were being re-examined internationally.
The aim was not only to prevent money laundering but also to allow for greater transparency about central bank help provided to banks experiencing liquidity problems.

"Apart from rendering bank officials unable to expose malpractices and abuses such as money laundering, this prohibition has on more than one occasion prevented the bank from exercising greater transparency or has rendered it powerless to respond to media reports," he said.
As a result, the bill proposed that the Finance Minister and the Reserve Bank governor could, after consultation with the client concerned, disclose such information.
This was in line with the freer flow of information at all levels worldwide and the fact that governments were becoming more concerned about the growth in money laundering.
"One must not lose sight, however, of the importance of ensuring that client-bank confidentiality is maintained," Manuel said.

The bill had originally given clients the chance to veto any disclosure but the parliamentary finance committee amended this so that they only had to consult the client concerned before giving their permission in writing.

"There have been arguments that the proposed amendment, providing for the unlimited disclosure of all information, even where this breaches the privileged relationship between the Reserve Bank and its clients, goes too far in remedying the current limtations.
"It must be noticed in this context that the power granted to the Minister of Finance and the Governor of the Reserve Bank are not absolute."

The Democratic Party, which originally had reservations about the amendment, on Tuesday withdrew its objection after being assured by the banks that they were happy with the proposed change and the discretion of the minister and governor.
